Un désaccord trop direct (« それは まちがいです »: Disagreeing too directly (“それは まちがいです”) sounds aggressive. Start by acknowledging the other point of view.

Bonne nouvelle : en espagnol, **chaque l: Good news: in Spanish, **every letter is pronounced**, always the same way (except **h**, which is always silent). Once you know the rules, you can read any word out loud.
L’alphabet a **27 lettres** : les 26 du: The alphabet has **27 letters**: the 26 of the English alphabet + **ñ**. The digraphs **ch**, **ll** and **rr** represent a single sound.
Pas de voyelles nasales, pas de « e » mu: No nasal vowels, no silent “e”: each vowel is short and clear.
**j** et **g** devant e/i : un « r » rac: **j** and **g** before e/i: a rasping sound from the back of the throat, like the “ch” in Scottish “loch”. **c** before e/i and **z**: English “th” in Spain, “s” in Latin America. **ll** and **y**: “y”. Single **r**: a tap of the tongue; **rr** or initial r: strongly rolled. **v** is pronounced like **b**.
Mot terminé par **voyelle, n ou s** : ac: Word ending in a **vowel, n or s**: stress on the **second-to-last** syllable (ca-sa, ha-blan). Otherwise: on the **last** one (ha-blar, ciu-dad). The **written accent** (á é í ó ú) marks an exception: ca-**fé**, **mú**-si-ca. It also distinguishes words: **sí** (yes) / si (if), **tú** (you) / tu (your).
